steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on adaptive constellation multiple access (ACMA) for beyond-5G wireless systems. Explain the limitations of NOMA (PD-NOMA with SIC, and phase-rotation schemes including joint detection) and then describe what ACMA does differently at the base station and the receiver.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. NOMA and PD-NOMA with SIC; their limitations
2. Phase-rotation schemes for NOMA (SIC-based and joint detection) and their limits
3. Our solution: ACMA (BS algorithm, MML receiver) and how we validate it

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. NOMA / PD-NOMA
- NOMA: share bandwidth among multiple users without subdividing time or frequency resources
- PD-NOMA: channel gain disparity + SIC to separate co-channel users' data; higher sum rates than OMA (e.g. OFDMA)
- SIC sensitive to co-channel users' signal power ratios; non-optimized ratios -> can't decode interference, error floor
- assumptions like high channel gain disparity may not hold in practical environments
- conventional NOMA not yet proven for sustained communication -> not in 3GPP work items

2. Phase rotation
- transmit signal phase rotation to improve detection with SIC and other methods
- one scheme: phase rotation for time diversity gain, block fading assumed, single-user receivers
- SIC beats single-user receivers when channel gains disparate
- other works: phase rotation optimization + SIC; but SIC treats other users' signals as noise -> limited gains with similar channel gains
- JD-NOMA: phase rotation + joint detection (JD) to address SIC limits
- limited to two users, [QPSK, QPSK] or [QPSK, 16-QAM], limited power allocation ratios; strict rules to cluster constellation points within I/Q axes boundary
- higher rotations -> very complicated detection boundaries, data hard to separate

3. ACMA
- power, modulation and phase agnostic; transmission + detection jointly minimize users' probability of error
- novel BS algorithm: unified composite signals, maximize distance of each neighbour point rather than clusters
- users' signal phases blind adaptively rotated to full potential using known powers and modulations
- not limited to small set of power/modulation choices (unlike JD-NOMA) -> diverse channel gain conditions
- MML based receiver: uses BS synergy + parameters shared via control channels, blindly finds/applies phase offsets -> best data rate and error performance
- superiority shown by extensive analyses and simulation results

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
NOMA is a promising way to share bandwidth among multiple users without dividing up time or frequency resources. A well-known variant is power-domain (PD)-NOMA, which relies on users having different channel gains and on the successive interference cancellation (SIC) method to separate the data of co-channel users, and it gives higher sum rates than orthogonal multiple access (OMA) such as OFDMA. The SIC method in PD-NOMA can be sensitive to the signal power ratios of the co-channel users. If the ratios are not optimized, it cannot decode the interference and it ends up with an error floor. Also, general assumptions in the NOMA literature, like users having high channel gain disparity, may not apply in a lot of practical wireless environments. So conventional NOMA is not yet proven to give sustained communication, which would be needed to be included as work items of 3GPP standards.

Phase rotation
- transmit signal phase rotation to improve detection with SIC and other methods
- one scheme: phase rotation for time diversity gain, block fading assumed, single-user receivers
- SIC beats single-user receivers when channel gains disparate
- other works: phase rotation optimization + SIC; but SIC treats other users' signals as noise -> limited gains with similar channel gains
- JD-NOMA: phase rotation + joint detection (JD); limited to two users, [QPSK, QPSK] or [QPSK, 16-QAM], limited power allocation ratios (strict clustering rules within I/Q axes boundary)
- higher rotations -> very complicated detection boundaries

ACMA
- power, modulation and phase agnostic; transmission + detection jointly minimize users' probability of error
- novel BS algorithm: unified composite signals, maximize distance of each neighbour point rather than clusters
- phases blind adaptively rotated to full potential using known powers and modulations
- unlike JD-NOMA, not limited to small set of power/modulation choices -> diverse channel gain conditions
- MML based receiver: BS synergy + parameters shared via control channels, blindly finds/applies phase offsets
- extensive analyses and simulation results

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
NOMA is a promising way to share bandwidth among multiple users without dividing up time or frequency resources. A well-known variant is power-domain (PD)-NOMA, which relies on users having different channel gains and on the successive interference cancellation (SIC) method to separate the data of co-channel users, and it gives higher sum rates than orthogonal multiple access (OMA) such as OFDMA. The SIC method in PD-NOMA can be sensitive to the signal power ratios of the co-channel users. If the ratios are not optimized, it cannot decode the interference and it ends up with an error floor. Also, general assumptions in the NOMA literature, like users having high channel gain disparity, may not apply in a lot of practical wireless environments. So conventional NOMA is not yet proven to give sustained communication, which would be needed to be included as work items of 3GPP standards.

Transmit signal phase rotation has been used for NOMA in earlier work to help improve detection with SIC and other methods. One scheme proposes phase rotation as a way to increase time diversity gain, assuming block fading of the underlying channels and using single-user receivers. It is known that SIC is better than single-user receivers when the channel gains of the users are disparate. Other works use phase rotation optimization together with SIC. But the SIC method treats the signals of the other users as noise, so their gains are limited when the users have similar channel gains. Phase rotation-based schemes that address the limitations of SIC with joint detection (JD), which we also call JD-NOMA here, have been proposed. But these are limited to two users with [QPSK, QPSK] or [QPSK, 16-QAM] setups, and to limited power allocation ratios for the users, because of strict rules for clustering constellation points within the boundary of the I/Q axes. If higher rotations are used, the receivers cannot easily separate the data, since their detection boundaries get very complicated.

We solve the issues of NOMA schemes with ACMA, which is agnostic to power, modulation and phase, and where the transmission and detection systems work together to minimize the probability of error for the users. We devise a new algorithm at the BS that forms unified composite signals, designed to maximize the distance between each of the neighbour points instead of clusters. Here the signal phases of the users are blind adaptively rotated up to their full potential, using the knowledge of powers and modulations that is already available. Unlike JD-NOMA it is not limited to a small set of power and modulation choices, so it suits diverse channel gain conditions. We also propose an effective MML based receiver that makes use of the synergy given by the BS and the parameters it shares via control channels, to blindly find and apply the correct phase offsets and give the best possible data rate and error performance. We show that ACMA is superior through extensive analyses and simulation results.

A well-known variant is power-domain (PD)-NOMA, which relies on users having different channel gains and on the successive interference cancellation (SIC) method to separate the data of co-channel users, and it gives higher sum rates than orthogonal multiple access (OMA) such as OFDMA [1], [3]. The SIC method in PD-NOMA can be sensitive to the signal power ratios of the co-channel users [4]. If the ratios are not optimized, it cannot decode the interference and it ends up with an error floor [1]. Also, general assumptions in the NOMA literature, like users having high channel gain disparity, may not apply in a lot of practical wireless environments. So conventional NOMA is not yet proven to give sustained communication, which would be needed to be included as work items of 3GPP standards [3].

Transmit signal phase rotation has been used for NOMA in earlier work to help improve detection with SIC and other methods [5] - [6]. One scheme [7] proposes phase rotation as a way to increase time diversity gain, assuming block fading of the underlying channels and using single-user receivers. It is known that SIC is better than single-user receivers when the channel gains of the users are disparate. Other works [5], [8] [6] use phase rotation optimization together with SIC. But the SIC method treats the signals of the other users as noise, so their gains are limited when the users have similar channel gains. Phase rotation-based schemes that address the limitations of SIC with joint detection (JD), which we also call JD-NOMA here, have been proposed [9], [10], [11]. But these are limited to two users with [QPSK, QPSK] or [QPSK, 16-QAM] setups, and to limited power allocation ratios for the users, because of strict rules for clustering constellation points within the boundary of the I/Q axes. If higher rotations are used, the receivers cannot easily separate the data, since their detection boundaries get very complicated.

We solve the issues of NOMA schemes with ACMA, which is agnostic to power, modulation and phase, and where the transmission and detection systems work together to minimize the probability of error for the users. We devise a new algorithm at the BS that forms unified composite signals, designed to maximize the distance between each of the neighbour points instead of clusters. Here the signal phases of the users are blind adaptively rotated up to their full potential, using the knowledge of powers and modulations that is already available. Unlike JD-NOMA it is not limited to a small set of power and modulation choices, so it suits diverse channel gain conditions. We also propose an effective MML based receiver that makes use of the synergy given by the BS and the parameters it shares via control channels, to blindly find and apply the correct phase offsets and give the best possible data rate and error performance. We show that ACMA is superior through extensive analyses and simulation results.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
NOMA is a promising method to share bandwidth among multiple users without subdividing time or frequency resources [1] - [2]. Power-domain (PD)-NOMA is a well-known variant that relies on the channel gain disparity of users and the successive interference cancellation (SIC) method to separate co-channel users' data, giving higher sum rates than orthogonal multiple access (OMA) such as OFDMA [1], [3]. The SIC method used in PD-NOMA can be sensitive to co-channel users' signal power ratios [4]. When the ratios are not optimized, it cannot decode the interference and ends up with an error floor [1]. Moreover, general assumptions in the NOMA literature, such as high channel gain disparity of users, may not hold in many practical wireless environments. As such, conventional NOMA is not yet proven to provide the sustained communication needed for inclusion as work items of 3GPP standards [3].

Transmit signal phase rotation for NOMA, to help improve detection using SIC and other methods, is adopted in [5] - [6]. The scheme in [7] proposes phase rotation as a means to increase time diversity gain, assuming block fading of the underlying channels while using single-user receivers. It is known that SIC outperforms single-user receivers when users' channel gains are disparate. The works [5], [8] [6] use phase rotation optimization with SIC. However, SIC treats other users' signals as noise, so their gains are limited when users have similar channel gains. Phase rotation-based schemes addressing the limitations of SIC with joint detection (JD)—referred to here as JD-NOMA—are proposed in [9], [10], [11]. But they are limited to two users with [QPSK, QPSK] or [QPSK, 16-QAM] setups and to limited power allocation ratios, due to strict rules for clustering constellation points within the boundary of the I/Q axes. If higher rotations are imposed, the receivers cannot easily separate data, as their detection boundaries become very complicated.

We solve the issues of NOMA schemes using a power, modulation and phase agnostic ACMA, where the transmission and detection systems work together to minimize users' probability of error. We devise a novel algorithm at the BS that forms unified composite signals designed to maximize the distance of each neighbour point rather than of clusters. Here users' signal phases are blind adaptively rotated up to their full potential, utilizing the already available knowledge of powers and modulations. Unlike JD-NOMA, it is not limited to a small set of power and modulation choices, which makes it suitable for diverse channel gain conditions. We also propose an effective MML based receiver that capitalizes on the synergy provided by the BS and the parameters it shares via control channels to blindly find and apply the correct phase offsets, giving the best possible data rate and error performance. We prove the superiority of ACMA through extensive analyses and simulation results.
